title: Probability Theory II
subject: Statistics

cards.prompt: Define Almost-sure equality class. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The equivalence relation identifying random variables that differ only on a probability-zero event while retaining version-sensitive pointwise distinctions.
required_concepts: The equivalence relation identifying random variables that differ only on a probability-zero event while retaining version-sensitive pointwise distinctions.
major_error_concepts: Replacing an almost-sure statement by an everywhere statement without choosing a version.

cards.prompt: Define Borel event structure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The sigma-field generated by open subsets of a metric state space and its distinction from the full power set.
required_concepts: The sigma-field generated by open subsets of a metric state space and its distinction from the full power set.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every subset of an uncountable state space is Borel.

cards.prompt: What claim does Convergence-mode counterexample suite refute, and why?
cards.definition: **Definition.** The smallest constructions showing failure of converses among almost-sure probability Lp and distributional convergence.
required_concepts: The smallest constructions showing failure of converses among almost-sure probability Lp and distributional convergence.
major_error_concepts: Giving examples whose claimed convergence mode was never verified.

cards.prompt: Define Convergence-mode implication graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem-directed arrows among almost-sure probability Lp and distributional convergence with space and integrability conditions explicit.
required_concepts: The theorem-directed arrows among almost-sure probability Lp and distributional convergence with space and integrability conditions explicit.
major_error_concepts: Drawing reverse arrows from intuition or finite-sample closeness.

cards.prompt: Define Distribution as pushforward probability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The measure on the state space obtained by assigning each measurable set the probability of its random-variable preimage.
required_concepts: The measure on the state space obtained by assigning each measurable set the probability of its random-variable preimage.
major_error_concepts: Calling a density the distribution when atoms or singular mass may exist.

cards.prompt: Define Dominated convergence for expectations. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that almost-sure convergence plus domination by one integrable variable gives integrability of the limit and convergence in L1 and expectation.
required_concepts: The theorem that almost-sure convergence plus domination by one integrable variable gives integrability of the limit and convergence in L1 and expectation.
major_error_concepts: Using boundedness separately at each index or convergence in distribution as domination.

cards.prompt: What is Fatou lower-bound theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It preserves a one-sided lower bound when passing a liminf through integration for nonnegative functions, making it a safe fallback when domination is unavailable; it gives neither equality nor the reverse inequality.
required_concepts: It preserves a one-sided lower bound when passing a liminf through integration for nonnegative functions, making it a safe fallback when domination is unavailable
it gives neither equality nor the reverse inequality.
major_error_concepts: Turning the inequality into equality or reversing its direction.

cards.prompt: State Fatou lower-bound theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For nonnegative measurable random variables X_n, E[liminf_n X_n] <= liminf_n E[X_n], with extended-real values allowed.
required_concepts: The X_n are nonnegative and measurable.
E[liminf X_n] <= liminf E[X_n].
Extended-real values are permitted.
major_error_concepts: Turning the inequality into equality or reversing its direction.

cards.prompt: Define Integrable random variable. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A measurable variable whose absolute expectation is finite so positive and negative parts yield a finite signed expectation.
required_concepts: A measurable variable whose absolute expectation is finite so positive and negative parts yield a finite signed expectation.
major_error_concepts: Calling a conditionally convergent improper integral an expectation.

cards.term: Lebesgue expectation of a nonnegative variable
cards.prompt: Define Lebesgue expectation of a nonnegative variable. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The supremum of integrals of dominated nonnegative simple variables with infinity allowed and monotonicity built into the definition.
required_concepts: The supremum of integrals of dominated nonnegative simple variables with infinity allowed and monotonicity built into the definition.
major_error_concepts: Subtracting two infinite expectations or using a Riemann density formula universally.

cards.prompt: Define Measurable random variable. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A function from the probability space to a measurable state space whose inverse image of every measurable target set is an event.
required_concepts: A function from the probability space to a measurable state space whose inverse image of every measurable target set is an event.
major_error_concepts: Checking numerical values while omitting inverse-image measurability.

cards.prompt: Define Monotone convergence for expectations. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem that increasing nonnegative measurable variables converge in expectation to their pointwise limit including the infinite case.
required_concepts: The theorem that increasing nonnegative measurable variables converge in expectation to their pointwise limit including the infinite case.
major_error_concepts: Using monotone convergence for an oscillating signed sequence.

cards.prompt: Define Probability-measure continuity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The continuity from below and from above under the finite-first-measure condition derived from countable additivity.
required_concepts: The continuity from below and from above under the finite-first-measure condition derived from countable additivity.
major_error_concepts: Applying continuity from above when the first set has infinite measure in a general measure setting.

cards.prompt: Define Probability sigma-field. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A collection of subsets containing the sample space and closed under complements and countable unions whose members are the measurable events.
required_concepts: A collection of subsets containing the sample space and closed under complements and countable unions whose members are the measurable events.
major_error_concepts: Checking only finite unions or treating every subset as automatically measurable.

cards.prompt: Define Probability-space Lp norm. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: For 1≤p<infinity, ||X||_p=(E|X|^p)^(1/p), and L^p consists of variables for which it is finite, modulo almost-sure equality. For p=infinity, ||X||_infinity is the essential supremum of |X|. The same expression for 0<p<1 is not in general a norm because the triangle inequality can fail.
required_concepts: The norm range is 1≤p≤infinity.
Finite-p norms use the pth absolute moment and infinity uses essential supremum.
Identify variables equal almost surely; p<1 needs quasi-norm terminology.
major_error_concepts: The expression (E|X|^p)^(1/p) is a norm for every positive p, including p=1/2.

cards.prompt: Define Sigma-field generated by observations. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The smallest sigma-field making a declared family of events or random variables measurable and therefore encoding exactly their available event information.
required_concepts: The smallest sigma-field making a declared family of events or random variables measurable and therefore encoding exactly their available event information.
major_error_concepts: Adding distinctions that the specified observations cannot reveal.

cards.prompt: Define Simple-random-variable approximation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The monotone approximation of a nonnegative measurable random variable by finite-valued measurable functions used to define the integral.
required_concepts: The monotone approximation of a nonnegative measurable random variable by finite-valued measurable functions used to define the integral.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a finite support or uniform pointwise error without construction.

cards.prompt: Define Truncation and tail control. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The replacement of an unbounded variable by bounded measurable clips together with an explicit argument that the discarded tail vanishes in the needed norm or probability.
required_concepts: First material clause: The replacement of an unbounded variable by bounded measurable clips together with an
Remaining material clause: explicit argument that the discarded tail vanishes in the needed norm or probability.
major_error_concepts: Clipping the data and silently treating the truncated law as unchanged.

cards.prompt: State the uniform-integrability tail criterion and distinguish it from bounded first moments.
cards.definition: A family of integrable variables {X_i} is uniformly integrable if lim_{K→infinity} sup_i E[|X_i| 1{|X_i|>K}]=0. One common tail cutoff must work across the whole family. Uniform integrability plus convergence in probability to X gives convergence in L¹. Bounded first moments alone are insufficient: n 1{U≤1/n}, with U uniform on (0,1), has mean 1 but no uniform tail control.
required_concepts: State the tail expectation with supremum over the family before the K limit.
A common cutoff controls all members.
Bounded first moments are not enough.
major_error_concepts: Uniform integrability means only that sup_i E|X_i| is finite.

cards.prompt: Define Adapted and predictable process distinction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** adaptedness meaning each present variable is measurable now and predictability meaning the next coefficient is measurable before its use under the declared discrete-time convention.
required_concepts: adaptedness meaning each present variable is measurable now
and predictability meaning the next coefficient is measurable before its use under the declared discrete-time convention.
major_error_concepts: Calling every adapted process predictable or using the current unseen increment.

cards.prompt: Define Almost-sure uniqueness of conditional expectation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The result that two integrable conditioning-measurable versions satisfying the defining event identities agree outside one null event.
required_concepts: The result that two integrable conditioning-measurable versions satisfying the defining event identities agree outside one null event.
major_error_concepts: Demanding pointwise equality on every null-set representative.

cards.prompt: Define Change-of-probability likelihood ratio. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: If Q is absolutely continuous with respect to P, write w=dQ/dP. For Q-integrable h, E_Q[h]=E_P[h w], and E_P[w]=1. To estimate a Q-expectation using P draws, use this Q-over-P weight. Finite variance of h w is needed for variance-based error claims, not for the expectation identity itself.
required_concepts: State Q absolutely continuous with respect to P and w=dQ/dP.
The weighted P-expectation equals the Q-expectation under integrability.
Finite variance is a separate requirement for variance-based precision statements.
major_error_concepts: To compute E_Q[h] using P samples, always weight by dP/dQ, and an infinite variance makes every expectation identity false.

cards.prompt: Define Conditional expectation as L2 projection. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The orthogonal projection of a square-integrable variable onto the closed subspace of square-integrable variables measurable under the conditioning information.
required_concepts: The orthogonal projection of a square-integrable variable onto the closed subspace of square-integrable variables measurable under the conditioning information.
major_error_concepts: Calling the projection causal regression or assuming an L2 conclusion for merely integrable targets.

cards.prompt: Define Conditional-expectation existence by Radon-Nikodym. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The construction applying Radon-Nikodym to the signed or finite measure mapping each conditioning event to the target integral.
required_concepts: The construction applying Radon-Nikodym to the signed or finite measure mapping each conditioning event to the target integral.
major_error_concepts: Claiming existence from finite-partition intuition alone.

cards.prompt: What is Conditional Jensen inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It applies convexity after conditioning and controls conditional transforms, projections, and martingale expressions; its almost-sure direction depends on convexity and the required conditional integrability.
required_concepts: It applies convexity after conditioning and controls conditional transforms, projections, and martingale expressions
its almost-sure direction depends on convexity and the required conditional integrability.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring conditional integrability or reversing the inequality for convex functions.

cards.prompt: State conditional Jensen's inequality with a sufficient finite-integrability hypothesis.
cards.definition: Let G be a sub-sigma-field, X integrable, and phi convex on an interval containing X almost surely. If phi(X) is integrable, then phi(E[X|G])≤E[phi(X)|G] almost surely. These are random variables defined up to null sets; the inequality reverses for a concave phi.
required_concepts: X and phi(X) are integrable and phi is convex on the relevant domain.
State phi(E[X|G])≤E[phi(X)|G].
The comparison holds almost surely, not necessarily for every chosen version at every point.
major_error_concepts: For convex phi, E[phi(X)|G]≤phi(E[X|G]) everywhere, regardless of versions.

cards.prompt: Define Conditional monotone and dominated convergence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: For a fixed sub-sigma-field G: if 0≤X_n increases almost surely to X, then E[X_n|G] increases almost surely to E[X|G], allowing infinity. If X_n→X almost surely and |X_n|≤Y for a single integrable Y, then E[X_n|G]→E[X|G] almost surely and in L¹. One bound Y must control the whole sequence; separate index-dependent bounds are insufficient.
required_concepts: Conditional monotone convergence uses a nonnegative increasing sequence and permits infinity.
Conditional dominated convergence uses one integrable dominator and almost-sure convergence.
The fixed-information conditional expectations have the stated almost-sure limits.
major_error_concepts: Any sequence of individually bounded variables permits almost-sure exchange with conditional expectation, even when no common integrable bound exists.

cards.prompt: Define Filtration as growing information. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An increasing indexed family of sigma-fields representing what is knowable by each time without requiring it to be generated by the observed process.
required_concepts: An increasing indexed family of sigma-fields representing what is knowable by each time without requiring it to be generated by the observed process.
major_error_concepts: Using future observations or identifying a filtration with one random variable.

cards.prompt: Define Finite-partition conditional expectation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The version constant on each positive-probability partition cell with value equal to the cell-conditioned average and arbitrary values on null cells.
required_concepts: The version constant on each positive-probability partition cell with value equal to the cell-conditioned average and arbitrary values on null cells.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by a null cell probability or returning one global scalar.

cards.term: Fubini theorem for integrable random functions: role
cards.prompt: What is Fubini theorem for integrable random functions used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It authorizes changing integration order and guarantees almost-everywhere finite sections for absolutely integrable signed functions, enabling iterated-expectation calculations; separate-looking finite integrals do not replace absolute product integrability.
required_concepts: It authorizes changing integration order and guarantees almost-everywhere finite sections for absolutely integrable signed functions, enabling iterated-expectation calculations
separate-looking finite integrals do not replace absolute product integrability.
major_error_concepts: Checking only that separate integrals appear finite or ignoring exceptional sections.

cards.term: Fubini theorem for integrable random functions
cards.prompt: State Fubini theorem for integrable random functions, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The equality and almost-everywhere existence of iterated integrals when the absolute product integral is finite.
required_concepts: The equality and almost-everywhere existence of iterated integrals when the absolute product integral is finite.
major_error_concepts: Checking only that separate integrals appear finite or ignoring exceptional sections.

cards.prompt: Define Independence of sigma-fields. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The factorization of probabilities for every finite choice of events from declared sigma-fields rather than only zero covariance or selected pairs.
required_concepts: The factorization of probabilities for every finite choice of events from declared sigma-fields rather than only zero covariance or selected pairs.
major_error_concepts: Checking one event pair or only expectations of the coordinates.

cards.prompt: Define Product probability construction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The measure on a product sigma-field agreeing with rectangular products and supporting jointly measurable random coordinates.
required_concepts: The measure on a product sigma-field agreeing with rectangular products and supporting jointly measurable random coordinates.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying marginal probabilities before constructing or assuming the joint law.

cards.prompt: State the pull-out property of conditional expectation under a sufficient bounded-factor hypothesis.
cards.definition: If X is integrable and Y is bounded and G-measurable, then E[YX|G]=Y E[X|G] almost surely. More general unbounded versions require appropriate integrability of the product. Independence from G does not make Y known under G and does not justify pulling it outside.
required_concepts: Y is G-measurable.
Bounded Y and integrable X are a sufficient hypothesis.
State E[YX|G]=Y E[X|G] almost surely.
major_error_concepts: Any Y independent of G can be pulled outside E[YX|G] as the random factor Y.

cards.prompt: Define Radon-Nikodym density derivative. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: Let mu and nu be sigma-finite positive measures on the same measurable space, with nu absolutely continuous with respect to mu. Then there is a nonnegative measurable f, unique mu-almost everywhere, such that nu(A)=integral_A f dmu for every measurable A. Write f=dnu/dmu. This is a density relative to a measure, not necessarily a pointwise ratio of ordinary real-valued densities.
required_concepts: Both measures are sigma-finite and nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu.
State nu(A)=integral_A f dmu for every measurable A.
The density is nonnegative and unique mu-almost everywhere.
major_error_concepts: Every pair of measures has dnu/dmu, including a point mass nu when mu is Lebesgue measure.

cards.prompt: Define Regular conditional law boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A probability-kernel version of conditioning on a random element whose existence depends on state-space regularity and whose values remain version-dependent on null observations.
required_concepts: A probability-kernel version of conditioning on a random element whose existence depends on state-space regularity
and whose values remain version-dependent on null observations.
major_error_concepts: Assuming regular conditional probabilities exist on arbitrary measurable spaces or are unique at null values.

cards.prompt: Define Sigma-field conditional expectation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A conditioning-sigma-field measurable integrable random variable whose integral over every conditioning event matches that of the target variable.
required_concepts: A conditioning-sigma-field measurable integrable random variable whose integral over every conditioning event matches that of the target variable.
major_error_concepts: Treating the result as a scalar or pointwise conditional density value.

cards.term: Tonelli theorem for nonnegative random functions: role
cards.prompt: What is Tonelli theorem for nonnegative random functions used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It permits order exchange for nonnegative measurable integrands even when the common integral is infinite, supporting safe decomposition before proving finiteness; it cannot legitimize signed infinity-minus-infinity expressions.
required_concepts: It permits order exchange for nonnegative measurable integrands even when the common integral is infinite, supporting safe decomposition before proving finiteness
it cannot legitimize signed infinity-minus-infinity expressions.
major_error_concepts: Requiring integrability unnecessarily or using the conclusion for signed infinity-minus-infinity expressions.

cards.term: Tonelli theorem for nonnegative random functions
cards.prompt: State Tonelli theorem for nonnegative random functions, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The equality of iterated and product integrals for a nonnegative jointly measurable function even when the value is infinite.
required_concepts: The equality of iterated and product integrals for a nonnegative jointly measurable function even when the value is infinite.
major_error_concepts: Requiring integrability unnecessarily or using the conclusion for signed infinity-minus-infinity expressions.

cards.prompt: Define Tower property under nested information. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The identity that conditioning first on finer information and then on a nested coarser sigma-field equals direct conditioning on the coarser information.
required_concepts: The identity that conditioning first on finer information and then on a nested coarser sigma-field equals direct conditioning on the coarser information.
major_error_concepts: Applying tower to nonnested sigma-fields in an arbitrary order.

cards.term: Almost-sure convergence of independent random series
cards.prompt: Define Almost-sure convergence of independent random series. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The convergence criterion for centered independent square-integrable terms with summable variances together with truncation variants for unbounded terms.
required_concepts: The convergence criterion for centered independent square-integrable terms with summable variances together with truncation variants for unbounded terms.
major_error_concepts: Using summable variances without independence or centering.

cards.prompt: Define Berry-Esseen rate qualification. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The uniform distribution-function approximation rate under independent summands and a finite third-absolute-moment control with constants and normalization stated.
required_concepts: The uniform distribution-function approximation rate under independent summands
and a finite third-absolute-moment control with constants and normalization stated.
major_error_concepts: Calling an asymptotic CLT an exact finite-sample confidence guarantee.

cards.prompt: Define Characteristic function of a law. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The characteristic function of a real random variable X is phi_X(t)=E[e^{itX}] for real t, where i^2=-1; it always exists, is bounded by one in modulus, and determines the law of X.
required_concepts: phi_X(t)=E[e^{itX}] with the imaginary unit i.
It exists for every real-valued random variable and determines its law.
accepted_variants: Fourier transform of the probability law
major_error_concepts: Confusing it with an MGF that may be infinite or dropping independence in the product.

cards.prompt: What is Continuous mapping theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It transfers weak convergence through continuous transformations and lets a limiting law be propagated to derived statistics; discontinuities carrying positive limit probability require a separate argument.
required_concepts: It transfers weak convergence through continuous transformations and lets a limiting law be propagated to derived statistics
discontinuities carrying positive limit probability require a separate argument.
major_error_concepts: Using a discontinuous map at an atom of the limiting law.

cards.prompt: State Continuous mapping theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The result transferring convergence in distribution through a map continuous on a set carrying full limit probability.
required_concepts: The result transferring convergence in distribution through a map continuous on a set carrying full limit probability.
major_error_concepts: Using a discontinuous map at an atom of the limiting law.

cards.prompt: What is First Borel-Cantelli lemma used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It turns summable event probabilities into an almost-sure statement that only finitely many events occur, a standard route from tail bounds to eventual behavior; it needs no independence and does not say no event ever occurs.
required_concepts: It turns summable event probabilities into an almost-sure statement that only finitely many events occur, a standard route from tail bounds to eventual behavior
it needs no independence and does not say no event ever occurs.
major_error_concepts: Adding an independence assumption or concluding an event never occurs.

cards.prompt: State First Borel-Cantelli lemma, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The conclusion that only finitely many events occur almost surely when the sum of their probabilities is finite without requiring independence.
required_concepts: The conclusion that only finitely many events occur almost surely when the sum of their probabilities is finite without requiring independence.
major_error_concepts: Adding an independence assumption or concluding an event never occurs.

cards.prompt: Define Independent Borel-Cantelli converse. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The result that infinitely many independent events occur almost surely when their probability sum diverges with exact independence scope explicit.
required_concepts: The result that infinitely many independent events occur almost surely when their probability sum diverges with exact independence scope explicit.
major_error_concepts: Applying the converse to dependent events from a divergent sum alone.

cards.term: Kolmogorov maximal inequality for partial sums: role
cards.prompt: What is Kolmogorov maximal inequality for partial sums used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It controls the entire maximum path of independent centered partial sums by their terminal variance and supports uniform and strong-law arguments; the independence and finite-variance structure are essential.
required_concepts: It controls the entire maximum path of independent centered partial sums by their terminal variance and supports uniform and strong-law arguments
the independence and finite-variance structure are essential.
major_error_concepts: Applying the bound to dependent or infinite-variance increments.

cards.term: Kolmogorov maximal inequality for partial sums
cards.prompt: State Kolmogorov's maximal inequality for centered independent partial sums.
cards.definition: Let X_1,...,X_n be independent, mean-zero, square-integrable real variables, and let S_k=sum_{i=1}^k X_i. For a>0, P(max_{1≤k≤n}|S_k|≥a)≤Var(S_n)/a²=(sum_{i=1}^n Var(X_i))/a². It controls all partial sums through time n, not just the terminal event.
required_concepts: Independent increments have mean zero and finite variances.
The event is the maximum absolute partial sum exceeding a positive threshold.
The bound is total variance divided by the squared threshold.
major_error_concepts: For arbitrary dependent increments, the maximum partial-sum probability is always bounded by the sum of individual variances divided by a.

cards.prompt: What is Kolmogorov three-series theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It gives an exact almost-sure convergence criterion for a series of independent variables by separating rare large jumps, truncated drift, and truncated variance; checking only one of the three series is insufficient.
required_concepts: It gives an exact almost-sure convergence criterion for a series of independent variables by separating rare large jumps, truncated drift, and truncated variance
checking only one of the three series is insufficient.
major_error_concepts: Checking only raw variances or changing truncation rules across conditions.

cards.prompt: State Kolmogorov three-series theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For independent real random variables X_n and any fixed c>0, sum_n X_n converges almost surely iff: sum_n P(|X_n|>c)<infinity; sum_n E[X_n 1{|X_n|<=c}] converges; and sum_n Var(X_n 1{|X_n|<=c})<infinity.
required_concepts: The X_n are independent and one fixed truncation level c>0 is used.
The large-jump probabilities sum: sum P(|X_n|>c)<infinity.
The truncated means form a convergent numerical series.
The truncated variances have finite sum.
These three conditions are equivalent to almost-sure convergence of sum X_n.
major_error_concepts: Checking only raw variances or changing truncation rules across conditions.

cards.prompt: What is Kolmogorov zero-one law used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It proves that events determined only by the remote tail of independent variables cannot have intermediate probability, reducing analysis to deciding which extreme occurs; the law itself does not determine whether that extreme is zero or one.
required_concepts: It proves that events determined only by the remote tail of independent variables cannot have intermediate probability, reducing analysis to deciding which extreme occurs
the law itself does not determine whether that extreme is zero or one.
major_error_concepts: Computing which of zero or one holds without another argument.

cards.prompt: State Kolmogorov zero-one law, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The theorem that every tail event of an independent sequence has probability zero or one.
required_concepts: The theorem that every tail event of an independent sequence has probability zero or one.
major_error_concepts: Computing which of zero or one holds without another argument.

cards.prompt: What does Levy's continuity theorem let characteristic-function limits establish, and what continuity check is essential?
cards.definition: Levy's continuity theorem lets characteristic-function limits prove convergence in distribution. Once characteristic functions converge pointwise and their limit is continuous at zero, the theorem guarantees that the limit is a probability-law characteristic function. It does not require identifying a familiar density; losing continuity at zero can instead signal probability mass escaping to infinity.
required_concepts: Use: turn transform convergence into weak convergence.
Key limitation: the pointwise limit must be continuous at zero.
A separately named limiting density is optional.
major_error_concepts: Pointwise transform convergence is enough even if the limit is discontinuous at zero.

cards.prompt: State Levy continuity theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: For real-valued laws with characteristic functions phi_n, suppose phi_n(t)→phi(t) for every real t and phi is continuous at 0. Then phi is itself the characteristic function of a probability law mu, and the laws converge weakly to mu. Conversely weak convergence to mu implies pointwise convergence of characteristic functions to phi_mu. Identifying mu by a familiar closed-form density is not required.
required_concepts: Pointwise convergence holds for every real transform argument.
Continuity of the limit at zero is required.
The theorem supplies both the limiting probability law and weak convergence.
major_error_concepts: Any pointwise limit of characteristic functions yields a probability-law limit even when it is discontinuous at zero.

cards.prompt: What is Lindeberg-Feller triangular-array theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It extends central-limit reasoning to nonidentically distributed triangular arrays by excluding asymptotically dominant increments through the Lindeberg condition; row-wise normalization and independence cannot be ignored.
required_concepts: It extends central-limit reasoning to nonidentically distributed triangular arrays by excluding asymptotically dominant increments through the Lindeberg condition
row-wise normalization and independence cannot be ignored.
major_error_concepts: Using only a maximum-variance heuristic or mixing rows in the normalization.

cards.prompt: State the sufficient Lindeberg central-limit theorem for centered row-wise independent triangular arrays.
cards.definition: For each n, let X_(n,1),...,X_(n,k_n) be independent mean-zero variables with finite variances, and set s_n²=sum_j E[X_(n,j)²]>0. If for every epsilon>0, s_n^(-2) sum_j E[X_(n,j)² 1{|X_(n,j)|>epsilon s_n}]→0, then sum_j X_(n,j)/s_n converges in distribution to N(0,1). This sufficient direction needs row-wise independence, not independence across different rows.
required_concepts: Rows contain independent centered finite-variance summands and are normalized by total standard deviation.
State the full truncated-square Lindeberg condition for every epsilon.
The standardized row sum converges to N(0,1).
major_error_concepts: It suffices that the largest variance is small, with no Lindeberg tail condition, for every row-independent triangular array.

cards.prompt: State the bounded-continuous, closed-set, open-set, and continuity-set criteria in Portmanteau's theorem.
cards.definition: For Borel probability laws mu_n,mu on a metric space, weak convergence is equivalent to integral f dmu_n→integral f dmu for every bounded continuous real f. Equivalent set tests are limsup_n mu_n(F)≤mu(F) for every closed F, liminf_n mu_n(G)≥mu(G) for every open G, and mu_n(A)→mu(A) for every Borel set A whose boundary has mu-measure zero. Arbitrary sets with charged boundaries need not have convergent probabilities.
required_concepts: Bounded continuous test-function expectations converge.
Closed sets give an upper limsup bound; open sets give a lower liminf bound.
Exact set-probability convergence is required at mu-continuity sets.
major_error_concepts: Weak convergence requires mu_n(A)→mu(A) for every Borel set, even when its boundary has positive limit mass.

cards.prompt: Define Prokhorov subsequence boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The metric-space compactness principle relating tightness to relative weak compactness under Polish or stated regularity assumptions.
required_concepts: The metric-space compactness principle relating tightness to relative weak compactness under Polish or stated regularity assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming convergence of the full sequence or using the theorem on an arbitrary measurable space.

cards.prompt: What is Slutsky combination theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It justifies replacing a random nuisance quantity by a probability limit when combining it continuously with a weakly convergent statistic, powering many plug-in asymptotics; arbitrary marginal weak limits do not imply the required joint behavior.
required_concepts: It justifies replacing a random nuisance quantity by a probability limit when combining it continuously with a weakly convergent statistic, powering many plug-in asymptotics
arbitrary marginal weak limits do not imply the required joint behavior.
major_error_concepts: Combining arbitrary marginal weak limits as if they were jointly convergent.

cards.prompt: State Slutsky's theorem and its sum, product, and qualified quotient consequences.
cards.definition: If X_n converges in distribution to X and Y_n converges in probability to a constant c, then (X_n,Y_n) converges jointly in distribution to (X,c). Hence X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c and X_nY_n to cX. If c≠0, the quotient X_n/Y_n converges in distribution to X/c wherever the quotient is defined, with any convention on vanishing-denominator events whose probabilities go to zero.
required_concepts: One limit is a constant attained in probability.
The joint limit permits sum and product formulas.
The quotient requires a nonzero limiting denominator.
major_error_concepts: Two arbitrary marginal weak limits always give a joint weak limit and a valid quotient, even when the denominator limit is zero.

cards.prompt: Define Tail sigma-field of a sequence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The intersection of sigma-fields generated by all sufficiently late coordinates representing events unchanged by every finite prefix.
required_concepts: The intersection of sigma-fields generated by all sufficiently late coordinates representing events unchanged by every finite prefix.
major_error_concepts: Calling an event tail merely because it concerns a large index.

cards.prompt: Define Tight family of probability laws. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that for every positive epsilon one compact set captures all but epsilon mass uniformly across the family.
required_concepts: The property that for every positive epsilon one compact set captures all but epsilon mass uniformly across the family.
major_error_concepts: Choosing a compact set separately after selecting each law.

cards.term: Truncation proof of a strong law
cards.prompt: What is the reusable proof idea behind Truncation proof of a strong law?
cards.definition: **Definition.** The proof architecture controlling rare large summands centered truncated sums and normalization to obtain almost-sure sample-average convergence under explicit moments.
required_concepts: The proof architecture controlling rare large summands centered truncated sums
and normalization to obtain almost-sure sample-average convergence under explicit moments.
major_error_concepts: Citing the law without matching moments independence and normalization.

cards.prompt: Define Weak convergence of probability laws. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The convergence tested by expectations of every bounded continuous function on the declared metric state space.
required_concepts: The convergence tested by expectations of every bounded continuous function on the declared metric state space.
major_error_concepts: Treating weak convergence as pointwise density or total-variation convergence.

cards.prompt: What is Bounded optional sampling theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It formalizes the preservation of martingale fairness under bounded stopping and supports stopped-process calculations; unbounded stopping times require additional integrability or uniform-integrability conditions.
required_concepts: It formalizes the preservation of martingale fairness under bounded stopping and supports stopped-process calculations
unbounded stopping times require additional integrability or uniform-integrability conditions.
major_error_concepts: Applying the theorem to unbounded times without additional control.

cards.prompt: State bounded optional sampling for two ordered discrete-time stopping times.
cards.definition: Let (M_n,F_n) be an integrable discrete-time martingale and let S≤T be stopping times bounded by one deterministic finite N. Then E[M_T|F_S]=M_S almost surely, and in particular E[M_T]=E[M_S]=E[M_0]. No claim for arbitrary unbounded stopping times follows without a separate integrability or uniform-integrability argument.
required_concepts: Use an integrable martingale and stopping times S≤T bounded by a deterministic N.
State E[M_T|F_S]=M_S almost surely.
Expectation preservation does not extend automatically to unbounded times.
major_error_concepts: Almost-sure finiteness alone lets any stopping time replace a deterministic time in E[M_T]=E[M_0].

cards.prompt: Define Convex transformation submartingale. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The conditional Jensen result that an integrable convex transform of a martingale is a submartingale when transformed integrability holds.
required_concepts: The conditional Jensen result that an integrable convex transform of a martingale is a submartingale when transformed integrability holds.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every nonlinear transform preserves the martingale equality.

cards.prompt: Define Doob conditional-expectation martingale. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The process obtained by conditioning one integrable terminal variable on each filtration level with tower property giving the martingale relation.
required_concepts: The process obtained by conditioning one integrable terminal variable on each filtration level with tower property giving the martingale relation.
major_error_concepts: Calling the original data sequence itself a martingale.

cards.prompt: State the normalized discrete-time Doob decomposition and its predictable compensator formula.
cards.definition: For an integrable submartingale X_n adapted to F_n, set A_0=0 and A_n=sum_{k=1}^n E[X_k-X_(k-1)|F_(k-1)]. Then A is predictable and nondecreasing, and M_n=X_n-A_n is a martingale. This decomposition X=M+A is unique up to almost-sure equality under the normalization A_0=0; M_0=X_0.
required_concepts: Normalize A_0=0.
Predictable increments are the conditional drifts.
The remaining process is a martingale and A is increasing for a submartingale.
major_error_concepts: A deterministic trend chosen by curve fitting always gives the unique Doob decomposition without a normalization or conditional-drift check.

cards.prompt: What is Doob maximal inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It converts terminal submartingale control into a bound on the largest earlier excursion and is central to pathwise and Lp convergence arguments; each form has exact positivity and exponent requirements.
required_concepts: It converts terminal submartingale control into a bound on the largest earlier excursion and is central to pathwise and Lp convergence arguments
each form has exact positivity and exponent requirements.
major_error_concepts: Applying the Lp form at p equal to one or to a process lacking submartingale structure.

cards.prompt: State Doob maximal inequality, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** If (X_k)_{k=0}^n is a nonnegative submartingale, then for lambda>0, P(max_{k<=n} X_k>=lambda) <= E[X_n]/lambda. If p>1 and X is a martingale, ||max_{k<=n}|X_k|||_p <= [p/(p-1)]||X_n||_p.
required_concepts: The weak tail form assumes a nonnegative submartingale and lambda>0.
P(max_{k<=n} X_k>=lambda) <= E[X_n]/lambda.
For a martingale and p>1, ||max |X_k|||_p <= [p/(p-1)]||X_n||_p.
major_error_concepts: Applying the Lp form at p equal to one or to a process lacking submartingale structure.

cards.prompt: Define Exponential-supermartingale Azuma argument. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The construction bounding conditional exponential moments of bounded martingale differences and optimizing Markov's inequality for a tail bound.
required_concepts: The construction bounding conditional exponential moments of bounded martingale differences and optimizing Markov's inequality for a tail bound.
major_error_concepts: Using independent-sum Chernoff algebra without adapted conditional bounds.

cards.prompt: What is Martingale almost-sure convergence theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It turns uniform one-sided expectation control into an almost-sure terminal limit, providing the convergence step for many martingale constructions; L1 convergence still needs stronger uniform-integrability control.
required_concepts: It turns uniform one-sided expectation control into an almost-sure terminal limit, providing the convergence step for many martingale constructions
L1 convergence still needs stronger uniform-integrability control.
major_error_concepts: Claiming L1 convergence without uniform integrability.

cards.prompt: State Martingale almost-sure convergence theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The theorem giving an almost-sure finite limit for a submartingale with uniformly bounded positive-part expectations or a specified standard variant.
required_concepts: The theorem giving an almost-sure finite limit for a submartingale with uniformly bounded positive-part expectations or a specified standard variant.
major_error_concepts: Claiming L1 convergence without uniform integrability.

cards.prompt: Define Martingale difference sequence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An adapted integrable increment sequence whose conditional mean given the preceding information is zero.
required_concepts: An adapted integrable increment sequence whose conditional mean given the preceding information is zero.
major_error_concepts: Treating uncorrelated increments as conditionally centered.

cards.term: Martingale Lp and L1 convergence upgrade
cards.prompt: Define Martingale Lp and L1 convergence upgrade. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The strengthening from almost-sure convergence to Lp or L1 under p-greater-than-one boundedness or uniform integrability respectively.
required_concepts: The strengthening from almost-sure convergence to Lp or L1 under p-greater-than-one boundedness or uniform integrability respectively.
major_error_concepts: Treating bounded expectations as uniform integrability.

cards.term: martingale with respect to a filtration
cards.prompt: Define martingale with respect to a filtration. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** An integrable process (M_n) adapted to (F_n) is a martingale when E[M_{n+1}|F_n]=M_n almost surely for every n; in continuous time the corresponding condition is E[M_t|F_s]=M_s for s<=t.
required_concepts: An integrable process (M_n) adapted to (F_n) is a martingale when E[M_{n+1}|F_n]=M_n almost surely for every n
in continuous time the corresponding condition is E[M_t|F_s]=M_s for s<=t.
major_error_concepts: Omitting a defining condition or confusing martingale with respect to a filtration with a neighboring concept.

cards.prompt: What claim does Optional-stopping failure counterexample refute, and why?
cards.definition: Let S_n be the simple symmetric random walk starting at 0, and stop at T=inf{n≥0:S_n=1}. The walk is a martingale and T is finite almost surely, but T is not bounded and E[T]=infinity. Since S_T=1 almost surely, E[S_T]=1 differs from E[S_0]=0. The stopped family S_(T∧n) is not uniformly integrable, so this does not contradict bounded or UI-qualified optional stopping.
required_concepts: Specify an integrable martingale and verify a stopping-time rule.
Show that naive unqualified expectation preservation fails, by unequal expectations or failure of the required terminal integrability.
Identify the missing stopping/integrability hypothesis; the first-hit random-walk example is illustrative, not mandatory.
major_error_concepts: First hitting +1 is a bounded stopping time, so the fair-walk example disproves bounded optional sampling.

cards.prompt: Define Optional stopping under uniform integrability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The extension allowing an unbounded stopping limit when the stopped family is uniformly integrable and converges to an integrable terminal value.
required_concepts: The extension allowing an unbounded stopping limit when the stopped family is uniformly integrable and converges to an integrable terminal value.
major_error_concepts: Using almost-sure finite stopping alone as sufficient.

cards.prompt: Define Predictable martingale transform. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The cumulative sum of predictable stakes times martingale differences which remains a martingale under explicit integrability or boundedness conditions.
required_concepts: The cumulative sum of predictable stakes times martingale differences which remains a martingale under explicit integrability or boundedness conditions.
major_error_concepts: Letting the stake depend on the same unseen increment.

cards.prompt: Define Stopped martingale process. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The process evaluated at the minimum of the current time and a stopping time which remains a martingale under ordinary discrete-time conditions.
required_concepts: The process evaluated at the minimum of the current time and a stopping time which remains a martingale under ordinary discrete-time conditions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the terminal stopped value is integrable for an unbounded horizon.

cards.prompt: Define the stopped sigma-field F_T for a discrete-time stopping time.
cards.definition: For a stopping time T relative to (F_n), the stopped sigma-field is F_T={A in F: A intersect {T≤n} is in F_n for every n}. It consists of events whose truth can be determined using information available by the time stopping occurs. For T taking the deterministic value m, this reduces to F_m under the ambient filtration convention.
required_concepts: State the event intersection condition for every deterministic n.
The definition represents information available at stopping.
Do not replace a genuinely random T by one fixed filtration index.
major_error_concepts: F_T always equals F_(E[T]), since the expected stopping time is the information time.

cards.prompt: Define Stopping time for a filtration. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** A random nonnegative integer or infinity whose event of having occurred by each time belongs to the information then available.
required_concepts: A random nonnegative integer or infinity whose event of having occurred by each time belongs to the information then available.
major_error_concepts: Using the future path or final maximum to decide the stopping time.

cards.prompt: Define Submartingale and supermartingale order. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The integrable adapted processes whose conditional next values are respectively at least or at most their present values almost surely.
required_concepts: The integrable adapted processes whose conditional next values are respectively at least or at most their present values almost surely.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the order or omitting integrability.

cards.prompt: What is Upcrossing inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It bounds repeated oscillations across any interval and supplies the pathwise mechanism behind submartingale convergence; bounded expectations alone do not directly establish pointwise convergence without this oscillation control.
required_concepts: It bounds repeated oscillations across any interval and supplies the pathwise mechanism behind submartingale convergence
bounded expectations alone do not directly establish pointwise convergence without this oscillation control.
major_error_concepts: Calling bounded expectation direct proof of pointwise convergence.

cards.prompt: State an upcrossing inequality for an integrable submartingale, defining the completed-crossing count.
cards.definition: Let X_0,...,X_n be an integrable submartingale and a<b. Let U_n[a,b] count completed successive passages from a value at most a to a later value at least b by time n. Then (b-a)E[U_n[a,b]]≤E[(X_n-a)^+]-E[(X_0-a)^+], where z^+=max(z,0). Uniform positive-part expectation control therefore bounds expected upcrossings, supporting almost-sure convergence arguments.
required_concepts: Use a submartingale and count completed low-to-high crossings of a<b.
State the positive-part expectation bound with factor b-a.
major_error_concepts: For every arbitrary integrable process, the number of upcrossings is deterministically at most its terminal expectation.

cards.prompt: What is Bernstein variance-sensitive inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It gives a finite-sample tail bound that uses both variance and a uniform increment cap, interpolating between Gaussian and large-deviation regimes; neither the bound nor an empirical-variance substitution survives without the stated assumptions.
required_concepts: It gives a finite-sample tail bound that uses both variance and a uniform increment cap, interpolating between Gaussian and large-deviation regimes
neither the bound nor an empirical-variance substitution survives without the stated assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the uniform bound or substituting empirical variance without a theorem.

cards.prompt: State a bounded-independent Bernstein inequality, declaring its variance and tail conventions.
cards.definition: Let X_1,...,X_n be independent mean-zero real variables with |X_i|≤b almost surely for a fixed b>0, and let v=sum_i E[X_i²]. For t>0, P(sum_i X_i≥t)≤exp(-t²/[2(v+bt/3)]). A two-sided version has at most twice this bound. The v term is the true total variance, not an arbitrary empirical variance substituted after observation.
required_concepts: Independent summands are centered and uniformly bounded.
Use total variance v and bound b in the exponent t²/[2(v+bt/3)].
A two-sided probability needs its corresponding factor or bound.
major_error_concepts: Bernstein's bound permits an arbitrary sample variance in place of v and holds for unbounded dependent variables.

cards.prompt: State the Chernoff upper-tail bound as an optimization over valid exponential tilts.
cards.definition: For a real X and threshold a, P(X≥a)≤inf_{t>0: M_X(t)<infinity} exp(-ta)M_X(t), where M_X(t)=E[e^(tX)]. This follows from Markov for each admissible positive tilt; the infimum need not be attained. A lower-tail version applies to -X. Independence is not required for this one-variable bound, but is used to factor an MGF of a sum.
required_concepts: Use exp(-ta)M_X(t) for positive admissible t.
Optimize with an infimum over the finite MGF domain.
Do not reverse the tail or assume independence for the primitive bound.
major_error_concepts: Any negative or positive tilt can be substituted into the same upper-tail bound without checking the MGF domain.

cards.prompt: What is Cramer large-deviation theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It identifies the exponential-scale decay rate of iid sample-mean deviations through a Legendre transform and provides open- and closed-set asymptotic bounds; the rate is not an exact finite-sample probability.
required_concepts: It identifies the exponential-scale decay rate of iid sample-mean deviations through a Legendre transform and provides open- and closed-set asymptotic bounds
the rate is not an exact finite-sample probability.
major_error_concepts: Reporting the exponential rate as an exact probability or omitting the speed.

cards.prompt: State Cramer's sample-mean large-deviation theorem, including its speed and open/closed set bounds.
cards.definition: Let X_i be iid real variables whose MGF is finite on a neighborhood of 0. Write Xbar_n=(sum_{i=1}^n X_i)/n and I(x)=sup_t{tx-log E[e^(tX_1)]}. Then for every closed F, limsup_n (1/n)log P(Xbar_n in F)≤-inf_{x in F}I(x); for every open G, liminf_n (1/n)log P(Xbar_n in G)≥-inf_{x in G}I(x). Use log 0=-infinity and inf empty=infinity. These are asymptotic bounds at speed n, not exact finite-n probabilities.
required_concepts: Use iid real variables with an MGF neighborhood of zero.
The rate is the convex conjugate of the log MGF.
Closed sets have the upper limsup bound and open sets the lower liminf bound after dividing log probability by n.
major_error_concepts: Cramer's theorem says P(Xbar_n in A)=exp(-n inf_A I) exactly for every n and every set A.

cards.prompt: Define the Cramer transform and distinguish its effective domain from the MGF's tilt domain.
cards.definition: For Lambda(t)=log E[e^(tX)], define I(x)=sup_{t in R}{tx-Lambda(t)}, taking Lambda(t)=infinity where the MGF is infinite. Equivalently restrict the supremum to finite-Lambda tilts. I is a lower-semicontinuous convex nonnegative extended-valued function. The set of x where I(x)<infinity is its own effective domain, which is not generally the same as the MGF tilt domain.
required_concepts: Define the log MGF Lambda and the supremum tx-Lambda(t).
Infinite-MGF tilts do not contribute finite candidates.
Distinguish the tilt domain from the rate function's x domain.
major_error_concepts: The rate function is inf_t{tx-Lambda(t)} and must be finite at every point where the MGF is finite.

cards.prompt: Define Doob-exposure bounded-differences method. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The construction of a martingale by revealing independent inputs and bounding each forecast change to obtain concentration for a function.
required_concepts: The construction of a martingale by revealing independent inputs and bounding each forecast change to obtain concentration for a function.
major_error_concepts: Applying coordinate bounds after adaptive data selection or without independent inputs.

cards.prompt: What is Freedman martingale inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It extends Bernstein-style variance-sensitive concentration to martingale differences using predictable quadratic variation, enabling adaptive-process tail control; observed variance is not automatically the required predictable quantity.
required_concepts: It extends Bernstein-style variance-sensitive concentration to martingale differences using predictable quadratic variation, enabling adaptive-process tail control
observed variance is not automatically the required predictable quantity.
major_error_concepts: Replacing predictable variation by observed variance without justification.

cards.prompt: State a scalar Freedman inequality using predictable quadratic variation and an upper increment bound.
cards.definition: Let S_n=sum_{k=1}^n D_k, S_0=0, where D_k are square-integrable martingale differences and D_k≤b almost surely for a deterministic b>0. Set V_n=sum_{k=1}^n E[D_k²|F_(k-1)]. For t>0 and v>0, P(there exists n≥0 with S_n≥t and V_n≤v)≤exp(-t²/[2(v+bt/3)]). This is an upper-tail bound using predictable variation; replacing V_n by the observed sum of squared increments requires separate theory.
required_concepts: Use martingale differences with a deterministic upper bound and zero initial sum.
Predictable variation is the sum of conditional second moments.
State the joint crossing-and-variation event and Bernstein-form exponent.
major_error_concepts: Freedman uses V_n=sum D_k² with no conditional expectation, and the same bound holds with any data-chosen increment cap.

cards.prompt: Define Gartner-Ellis theorem preview. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The differentiability-and-steepness-qualified route from limiting scaled log MGFs to a large-deviation principle with exposed-point caveats retained.
required_concepts: The differentiability-and-steepness-qualified route from limiting scaled log MGFs to a large-deviation principle with exposed-point caveats retained.
major_error_concepts: Assuming existence of a limiting log MGF automatically gives a full LDP.

cards.term: Hoeffding inequality for bounded independent sums: role
cards.prompt: What is Hoeffding inequality for bounded independent sums used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It supplies a distribution-free exponential deviation bound from independent bounded ranges and supports nonasymptotic confidence and learning guarantees; dependence or mere finite variance falls outside its contract.
required_concepts: It supplies a distribution-free exponential deviation bound from independent bounded ranges and supports nonasymptotic confidence and learning guarantees
dependence or mere finite variance falls outside its contract.
major_error_concepts: Using the inequality for dependent or merely finite-variance variables.

cards.term: Hoeffding inequality for bounded independent sums
cards.prompt: State one-sided and two-sided Hoeffding bounds for a centered sum of independent bounded variables.
cards.definition: Let X_1,...,X_n be independent with a_i≤X_i≤b_i almost surely, and let D=sum_i(b_i-a_i)²>0. For t>0, P(sum_i(X_i-E[X_i])≥t)≤exp(-2t²/D). Applying the bound to both signs gives P(|sum_i(X_i-E[X_i])|≥t)≤2exp(-2t²/D), optionally capped at 1. Identical distributions are not required; if D=0 the centered sum is identically zero.
required_concepts: The variables are independent and have declared almost-sure finite ranges.
Use the centered sum and denominator sum of squared range lengths.
One-sided exponent is -2t²/D; a two-sided bound may add the factor 2.
major_error_concepts: Identical bounded marginals suffice for Hoeffding even when every summand is the same random variable and thus fully dependent.

cards.prompt: What is Large-deviation contraction principle used for, and what is its main limitation?
cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It propagates a large-deviation principle through a continuous map and obtains the transformed rate by minimizing over preimages, allowing derived quantities to inherit exponential asymptotics; ordinary weak convergence is too weak for this conclusion.
required_concepts: It propagates a large-deviation principle through a continuous map and obtains the transformed rate by minimizing over preimages, allowing derived quantities to inherit exponential asymptotics
ordinary weak convergence is too weak for this conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Using ordinary weak continuous mapping without exponential-scale control.

cards.prompt: State a good-rate version of the large-deviation contraction principle and its transformed rate formula.
cards.definition: Suppose laws of X_n on a Polish space satisfy an LDP at speed a_n→infinity with good rate function I, and T is continuous into another Polish space. Then T(X_n) satisfies an LDP at the same speed, with good rate J(y)=inf_{x:T(x)=y}I(x); the empty-preimage infimum is infinity. Ordinary weak convergence alone does not supply an LDP.
required_concepts: Start with an LDP and good rate I on the stated spaces.
T is continuous and the speed stays the same.
Minimize I over each preimage, assigning infinity to an empty preimage.
major_error_concepts: A continuous transformation of any weakly convergent sequence automatically has an LDP, with rate J(y)=I(T(y)).

cards.prompt: Define Qualified Probability Theory II conclusion. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The narrow statement supported by exact probability spaces hypotheses proofs counterexamples and reviews with learner empirical research deployment and downstream claims denied.
required_concepts: The narrow statement supported by exact probability spaces hypotheses proofs counterexamples
and reviews with learner empirical research deployment and downstream claims denied.
major_error_concepts: Calling course artifact completion advanced-probability mastery or research readiness.

cards.prompt: Define Rare-event importance-sampling evidence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The change-of-measure estimator with likelihood ratio unbiasedness finite-variance condition and efficiency criterion separated from the exact target probability.
required_concepts: The change-of-measure estimator with likelihood ratio unbiasedness finite-variance condition
and efficiency criterion separated from the exact target probability.
major_error_concepts: Using reversed weights or claiming lower variance without analysis.

cards.prompt: Define Sanov empirical-measure preview. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The large-deviation principle for empirical measures with relative entropy rate under topology and support conditions delegated to the exact theorem.
required_concepts: The large-deviation principle for empirical measures with relative entropy rate under topology and support conditions delegated to the exact theorem.
major_error_concepts: Treating KL as symmetric distance or absorbing information theory into this course.

cards.prompt: Distinguish Stochastic simulation versus theorem evidence.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The distinction among exact law calculation proved bound asymptotic rate and Monte Carlo estimate with random seed sample size uncertainty and failure count retained.
required_concepts: The distinction among exact law calculation proved bound asymptotic rate
and Monte Carlo estimate with random seed sample size uncertainty and failure count retained.
major_error_concepts: Using simulation agreement as proof of measurability independence convergence or mixing.

cards.prompt: Define Stochastic theorem support graph. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
cards.definition: **Definition.** The row-complete support graph from probability spaces and measurable integrals through conditional identities convergence modes filtrations stopping controls or process constructions to one exact stochastic conclusion.
required_concepts: First material clause: The row-complete support graph from probability spaces and measurable integrals through conditional identities
Remaining material clause: convergence modes filtrations stopping controls or process constructions to one exact stochastic conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Summarizing the probability argument by theorem name or simulation output.

cards.prompt: Define the centered sub-Gaussian MGF condition using a variance proxy, and distinguish it from Gaussianity.
cards.definition: A centered real variable X is sigma²-sub-Gaussian in the variance-proxy convention if E[exp(tX)]≤exp(sigma²t²/2) for every real t. The proxy sigma² bounds the variance but need not equal it, and the inequality does not imply X is Gaussian. A conditional version requires the corresponding conditional MGF bound almost surely given a specified sigma-field.
required_concepts: The variable is centered and the MGF bound holds for every real t.
State the factor sigma²t²/2.
The proxy is not an assertion of a Gaussian law or necessarily the exact variance.
major_error_concepts: Every centered finite-variance variable is sub-Gaussian with proxy exactly equal to its variance.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in Probability Theory II.
